section.title: Eliphaz's Third Speech
section.sectionRationale: This is Eliphaz's last word, and it is his harshest. In the first cycle he was gentle, in the second he grew sharper, and now, unable to answer Job's arguments, he abandons restraint altogether and simply invents a list of crimes against him. It is the clearest sign in the whole book that a theology which cannot explain the evidence in front of it will eventually manufacture evidence to fit the theology.
section.thesis: When a fixed doctrine of retribution meets a reality it cannot account for, it does not bend, it accuses; Eliphaz wraps true words about God's greatness and the call to reconcile around fabricated charges he has no grounds to bring against an innocent man.
section.frameNote: Four movements: Eliphaz's opening question of whether a man's righteousness could ever benefit God; his invented list of Job's supposed crimes against the vulnerable; a theology of God's transcendence twisted to excuse presumption; and a closing appeal to reconcile and be restored that is true in general yet wrongly aimed at Job.

verses.text: Then Eliphaz the Temanite replied:
“Can a man be of use to God? Can even a wise man benefit Him?
Does it delight the {{shaddai|Almighty}} that you are righteous? Does He profit if your ways are blameless?
Is it for your reverence that He {{yakach|rebukes}} you and enters into judgment against you?
Is not your wickedness great? Are not your iniquities endless?
For you needlessly demanded security from your brothers and deprived the naked of their clothing.
You gave no water to the weary and withheld food from the famished,
while the land belonged to a mighty man, and a man of honor lived on it.
You sent widows away empty-handed, and the strength of the fatherless was crushed.
Therefore snares surround you, and sudden peril terrifies you;
it is so dark you cannot see, and a flood of water covers you.

units.label: A theology of distance twisted
units.note: God is so high He cannot see, they say

verses.text: Is not God as high as the heavens? Look at the highest stars, how lofty they are!
Yet you say: ‘What does God know? Does He judge through thick darkness?
Thick clouds veil Him so He does not see us as He traverses the vault of heaven.’
Will you stay on the ancient path that wicked men have trod?
They were snatched away before their time, and their foundations were swept away by a flood.
They said to God, ‘Depart from us. What can the Almighty do to us?’
But it was He who filled their houses with good things; so I stay far from the counsel of the wicked.
The righteous see it and are glad; the innocent mock them:
‘Surely our foes are destroyed, and fire has consumed their excess.’
Reconcile now and be at {{shalom|peace}} with Him; thereby good will come to you.
Receive instruction from His mouth, and lay up His words in your heart.
If you return to the Almighty, you will be restored. If you remove injustice from your tents
and consign your gold to the dust and the gold of Ophir to the stones of the ravines,
then the Almighty will be your gold and the finest silver for you.
Surely then you will delight in the Almighty and lift up your face to God.
You will pray to Him, and He will hear you, and you will fulfill your vows.
Your decisions will be carried out, and {{or|light}} will shine on your ways.
When men are brought low and you say, ‘Lift them up!’ then He will save the lowly.
He will deliver even one who is not innocent, rescuing him through the cleanness of your hands.”

shaddai.gloss: The Almighty, a divine title used throughout Job more than anywhere else in the Old Testament. It stresses overwhelming power, which is exactly what Eliphaz appeals to: surely such a God has no need of, and takes no note of, one man's righteousness or sin.

yakach.gloss: To rebuke, reason, or argue a case, often in a legal setting. Eliphaz asks whether God enters this kind of courtroom dispute with Job over his reverence; the same root recurs across Job for the case Job wants to argue before God, 13:3, 23:7.

shalom.gloss: Peace, wholeness, well-being. Eliphaz's call to 'be at peace with Him' is true wisdom in itself, echoed throughout Scripture, but here it is aimed at a man who has done nothing to be reconciled from.

or.gloss: Light. Eliphaz promises Job that light will shine on his ways if he repents, the same word used of the light God speaks into darkness, and the very thing Job feels he has lost, 19:8, 23:17.

basic.context: This is Eliphaz's third and final speech, and it is a shock. In his first two speeches he spoke in generalities about sin and suffering. Now, unable to answer Job's case, he simply invents specific crimes: robbing the naked, starving the hungry, crushing widows and orphans. Nothing in the story supports any of this. He is not reporting facts; he is forcing Job to fit his theology.
basic.hermeneutics: The chapter is honest about how good theology curdles into cruelty when it must be defended at all costs. Eliphaz's opening question and his closing appeal both contain real truth, God's self sufficiency, the goodness of returning to Him, but the middle section shows a man so committed to his system that he will lie to keep it standing. Job later swears under oath that these very charges are false, 31:16-22.
basic.originalLanguages: Eliphaz invokes Shaddai, the Almighty, a title that dominates Job, to argue that God is too great to be affected by human righteousness or sin, and therefore Job's suffering must be punishment for real crimes. He uses yakach, the courtroom word for arguing a case, the same word Job has used to long for his day in court. And he promises Job that or, light, will return if he repents, unaware that Job already walks in a darkness no repentance from invented sin could lift.
basic.typology: Job stands here as a righteous man falsely accused by those who claim to speak for God, a pattern that reaches its fullest form in Jesus, accused of blasphemy and sedition by the very religious leaders who should have recognized Him. The false friend who wounds in the name of truth anticipates every accuser who uses God's name to justify cruelty.
basic.christ: Eliphaz's fabricated charges against an innocent man foreshadow the false testimony brought against Jesus, who also had done nothing to deserve His suffering and was condemned by men certain they were serving God. Job's silence under false accusation, and his eventual vindication in chapter 42, points toward the greater silence and greater vindication of Christ.
basic.god: God does not need Job's righteousness, Eliphaz is right about that, yet God is not distant or blind as Eliphaz's fabricated evidence and the friends' whole system implies. The book will show that God sees, cares, and eventually rebukes Eliphaz himself for these very words, 42:7.
basic.crossReferences: Job 31:16-22 has Job deny under oath every charge Eliphaz invents here. Psalm 34:14 and Proverbs 3:7 echo the true counsel buried in verses 21-27. Matthew 26:59-61 shows false witnesses inventing charges against Jesus much as Eliphaz invents them against Job.
basic.oneStory: Eliphaz's speech is theology weaponized: true things about God's greatness and the goodness of returning to Him, wrapped around lies invented to protect a broken system. The Bible's answer to this kind of religious cruelty is Christ, falsely accused and finally vindicated, who exposes every attempt to use God's name to crush the innocent.

context.literary:
Eliphaz spoke first in the book, at the head of the first cycle, and he speaks last in the dialogue proper, since Bildad's third speech is only six verses and Zophar is silent. The speeches show a steady hardening. In chapters 4 and 5 he began with courtesy and a night vision; in chapter 15 he became sharp; here he drops the general language altogether and says 'you.'

The speech is arranged in four turns. It opens with rhetorical questions about God's independence, verses 2 to 5, whose last question, 'Is not your wickedness great?', is the hinge. Verses 6 to 11 supply the evidence, a list of sins introduced with 'For,' and then draw a consequence with 'Therefore,' verse 10. Verses 12 to 20 turn to a claim about what Job believes, quoting words that Job has never said. And verses 21 to 30 change tone entirely, into the most tender appeal in the friends' speeches, a string of conditional promises.

The logic runs backward, and the structure shows it. Job's calamity comes first in the story, and the crimes are then inferred to explain it. The 'Therefore' of verse 10 is not evidence of a link but the moment the argument admits it has none. Snares, sudden peril, darkness and a flood, verses 10 and 11, are the description of Job's actual situation, offered as proof that he must have done something to earn it.

Two verbal echoes carry the speech. The root behind 'of use' in verse 2 returns in verse 21, and the Almighty appears again and again, five times in all, in verses 3, 17, 23, 25 and 26. The name that opens the sermon as a distant Judge closes it as a friend to delight in, and the reader hears Eliphaz begin to believe his own promises.
context.historical:
Eliphaz is a Temanite, and Teman was in Edom, a region the prophets remembered for its wisdom, Jeremiah 49:7 and Obadiah 8. His speech is the voice of the wise man as the ancient world understood him: an elder, secure in received tradition, sure that moral cause and effect can be read off the surface of life.

The sins he lists are the classic offences of a powerful man in an agrarian society, and each has a matching law. Taking a pledge from a brother and stripping the poor of clothing recalls the rule that a cloak taken as security must be returned by sundown, because it is the only covering the poor man has, Exodus 22:26-27 and Deuteronomy 24:12-13. Refusing water and bread to the weary breaks the law of hospitality that runs through Genesis. Sending widows away empty-handed and crushing the fatherless offends against what the Law calls the LORD's special concern, Exodus 22:22-24 and Deuteronomy 27:19. The prophets later charge Israel with these same sins, Isaiah 10:1-2 and Amos 2:6-8.

Verse 8 is difficult, and the words 'the land belonged to a mighty man, and a man of honor lived on it' may describe Job himself as the powerful landowner who used his standing against the poor, or the wealthy class Job is accused of favouring. Either way, it belongs to a world where land and status were bound together.

The gold of Ophir, verse 24, was the proverbial best gold, brought by Solomon's fleets, 1 Kings 9:28. To cast it into the stones of the ravines means to throw the most precious thing into the stream bed among the pebbles. And the picture of a God veiled in 'thick darkness,' verses 13 and 14, borrows from Israel's own tradition, where the LORD was said to dwell in thick darkness, Exodus 20:21 and 1 Kings 8:12. Eliphaz uses a real theme to make a false accusation.
context.canonical:
Job answers this chapter with one of the longest passages in the book. In chapter 31 he swears an oath, item by item, against exactly these sins, including denying the desires of the poor, letting the widow's eyes fail, and seeing someone perish for lack of clothing, Job 31:16-22. He even says, 'may my arm fall from my shoulder,' which answers Eliphaz's picture of the mighty man's arm and the crushed arm of orphans. In the epilogue God says that Eliphaz and his friends have not spoken accurately about Him, and tells them to ask Job to pray for them, Job 42:7-9.

The rest of Scripture treats the sins as real and serious. Isaiah says the true fast is to share bread with the hungry, bring the poor into your home and clothe the naked, Isaiah 58:6-7. Proverbs says 'Kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD,' Proverbs 19:17. And Jesus makes these very acts the test at the last judgment: 'I was hungry and you gave Me something to eat... I was naked and you clothed Me,' Matthew 25:35-36. The difference is that Jesus names them as the marks of those who are welcomed, and the acts are the fruit of a life already in His care.

Eliphaz's claim that God gains nothing from a man's righteousness is echoed by Elihu, Job 35:6-8, and is a true statement in itself: 'Nor is He served by human hands, as if He needed anything,' Acts 17:25, and 'Who has first given to God, that God should repay him?' Romans 11:35. But the New Testament uses this truth to show grace, not to prove that God does not care what people do. And the picture of a God who cannot see is what the wicked say in Psalm 10:11 and 94:7, and what God answers in Psalm 94:9 and Jeremiah 23:24.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author lets the most respectable of the friends make the most disgraceful move: he invents evidence. Readers who knew from the prologue that Job was blameless, 1:8 and 2:3, are meant to see that Eliphaz is no longer an observer but an advocate, and that a man defending an idea will say whatever the idea needs. The list of crimes in verses 6 to 9 is placed in the text so that it can be refuted by Job's own oath in chapter 31.

He also wanted the audience to feel how close the speech comes to wisdom. Eliphaz's first three verses are true, since no human righteousness can add to God, and his last ten verses are among the loveliest appeals in the book, urging a man to receive instruction from God's mouth, lay up His words in the heart, and delight in the Almighty. The sting is that the whole invitation depends on the premise that Job is guilty. The author shows that truth, when fastened to a false charge, becomes a weapon.

A quieter purpose is to prepare for the ending. Eliphaz says in verse 30 that a man not innocent will be delivered through the cleanness of another's hands, and the author will bring that sentence true in a way Eliphaz never intended: at the end of the book Job's prayer is what saves the friends from God's wrath, 42:8-9.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records the words of a man God later calls inaccurate, and none of its charges is a fact of the story. It cannot be quoted as though it were the book's own account of Job. The verses of promise in 21 to 30 are likewise Eliphaz's conditional offer, not a divine covenant, and the book takes care to show that Job's restoration in chapter 42 comes on God's terms and not because he followed this formula.

Yet there are principles worth carrying. The list of sins is a checklist of what the Law and the prophets condemn, and it is right for any believer with wealth or power to ask whether a pledge is being held too long, whether the hungry are fed, and whether widows and the fatherless are heard. James makes the same point when he says faith without meeting a brother's bodily needs is worthless, James 2:15-16.

The appeal to return to God and delight in Him is also good counsel in its place. Where there is actual sin, the New Testament says to confess it, 1 John 1:9. What the chapter forbids is the move from a general truth to a specific accusation without evidence. Speaking for God carries a duty of truthfulness, and that duty is heaviest when the person in front of you is suffering.

debates.question: Is Eliphaz lying, or does he honestly believe Job is guilty?

views.label: A deliberate fabrication
views.case: The charges appear from nowhere, with no witness and no prior hint in the dialogue. God says in 42:7 that the friends have not spoken accurately of Him. On this view Eliphaz manufactures evidence to keep his system intact.

views.label: A sincere inference from his theology
views.case: Eliphaz holds that suffering proves sin, so he reasons that Job must have committed the kinds of sin a rich man would commit. He may believe it, having convinced himself, and be blind to his own reasoning. His mistake is a false premise, not a conscious lie.

debates.bearing: The text does not settle his motive, but it does settle his fault. Either way he bears false witness, and the book treats the result as serious enough that he needs Job's prayer and a burnt offering, 42:8.

debates.question: Does verse 30 promise that the pure can rescue the guilty?

views.label: Deliverance through another's intercession
views.case: The BSB reads 'He will deliver even one who is not innocent, rescuing him through the cleanness of your hands.' The plain sense is that a righteous man's prayer can rescue the guilty. Job 42:8 and Genesis 18 support the idea of an intercessor.

views.label: An obscure line, possibly 'the island of the innocent'
views.case: The Hebrew phrase is difficult, and some older translations read the words as naming a place or the innocent themselves, so that God delivers 'the innocent' through the purity of Job's hands. Under that reading the promise is only that a restored Job will be a blessing to others.

debates.bearing: Whichever reading is followed, the verse says that Job's clean hands can be a channel of rescue. The book fulfils it in an ironic way, since Job, the man Eliphaz calls guilty, does intercede for the friends.

study.originalLanguages:
The speech is stitched together by a small word game. In verse 2 Eliphaz asks whether a man can be 'of use' to God, using a Hebrew verb that means to be of benefit, and in verse 21 the imperative 'Reconcile' comes from the same root. The verb in verse 21 is a form that means to make oneself familiar, to become acquainted, so the appeal is literally to 'get to know Him.' The sermon begins by saying God has no need of human usefulness and ends by asking Job to become familiar with God. It is a small mark of the speech's unity, and of the tension inside it: God needs nothing, yet Job is urged to draw near.

The title Shaddai, the Almighty, occurs five times in the BSB of this chapter, in verses 3, 17, 23, 25 and 26. In Job it is the name most associated with God's overwhelming power, and Eliphaz places it at both ends of his speech. It first appears as the God who is unmoved by Job's righteousness, and it is the God to whom Job is told to return, in whom he will find delight.

Verse 4 uses the courtroom verb for reproving, translated 'rebukes,' and pairs it with 'enters into judgment.' The question, 'Is it for your reverence that He rebukes you?', treats Job's piety as a bargaining chip and asks whether God would punish him for it. The question echoes the accuser's challenge in the prologue, 'Does Job fear God for nothing?' 1:9. The idea that piety must pay, or that it cannot, sits behind both.

In verse 6 the phrase 'demanded security' rests on the verb for taking a pledge, the same verb that governs the law about the cloak in Exodus 22:26 and Deuteronomy 24:6 and 24:17, and Job uses the same root later in 24:3 for those who take a widow's ox in pledge. Eliphaz has chosen a precise legal offence, one the reader can check against the Torah.

Verse 8 pictures power by the arm. The Hebrew describes the mighty man as a man of arm and the honoured one as one whose face is lifted, and in verse 9 the 'strength' of the fatherless is the same word, arm, so their arms are crushed. Arm is the ancient picture of strength, and Job answers in 31:22 with 'may my arm fall from my shoulder.'

The BSB footnote on verse 14 notes that the 'vault of heaven' can also be 'heaven's horizon or the circle of the sky.' The Hebrew word describes a circle, and Isaiah 40:22 uses the related idea of the circle of the earth. Eliphaz has God pacing around the rim of the sky, hidden by cloud, while Job supposedly says He cannot see.

In verse 23 the promise 'you will be restored' comes from a verb meaning to be built up, so the house of Job is imagined as rebuilt. Verse 28 says light 'will shine' on his ways, with a verb that Isaiah 9:2 uses for light dawning on people in darkness. Finally, verse 30 depends on a hard phrase, which the BSB renders 'one who is not innocent.' Some older translations take the same Hebrew letters as 'the island of the innocent,' and the ambiguity is a warning that this line should be handled with care.

typology.type: The false accuser and the just man, Job 22:5-9
typology.fulfillment: Eliphaz brings accusations that no one can prove against a man of integrity. At Jesus' trial 'the chief priests and the whole Sanhedrin were seeking false testimony against Jesus,' and though many false witnesses came, they did not agree, Matthew 26:59-61. Like Job, Jesus is accused by the religious, in the name of God, of what He has not done. The escalation is that Jesus, unlike Job, gave no answer, Matthew 27:12-14, and 'entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly,' 1 Peter 2:23. The correspondence falls short in that Job protests his innocence while Christ, the truly sinless one, bears the accusation in silence for others.

typology.type: Peace with God through a mediator, Job 22:21
typology.fulfillment: Eliphaz urges Job to 'be at peace' with God. The desire is good, and the New Testament shows how peace is made. 'He Himself is our peace,' Ephesians 2:14, and God has been pleased 'to reconcile to Himself all things... by making peace through the blood of His cross,' Colossians 1:20. Paul concludes, 'since we have been justified through faith, we have peace with God,' Romans 5:1. The escalation is decisive: Eliphaz makes peace a result of Job's own repentance and effort, while the gospel makes it a gift from Christ. The type falls short because it puts the burden on the sinner.

typology.type: The clean hands that rescue the guilty, Job 22:30
typology.fulfillment: Eliphaz says God will rescue even one who is not innocent 'through the cleanness of your hands.' The book fulfils this at the end when Job prays for the friends and God accepts his prayer, 42:8-9. The pattern reaches its height in Christ, who 'always lives to intercede' for those who come to God through Him, Hebrews 7:25, and who 'bore the sin of many and made intercession for the transgressors,' Isaiah 53:12. The type falls short because Job's hands, though clean of the charges, are not spotless in himself, while Christ's righteousness is perfect.

typology.type: Treasure worth more than gold, Job 22:24-25
typology.fulfillment: Eliphaz tells Job to cast his gold to the ravines and let the Almighty be his gold. Behind the claim is an old truth that the Bible repeats. Jesus says treasures on earth are corruptible and treasures in heaven are safe, and 'where your treasure is, there your heart will be also,' Matthew 6:19-21. Paul counts everything as loss 'compared to the surpassing excellence of knowing Christ Jesus,' Philippians 3:7-8. The escalation is that God does not merely replace the treasure but gives Himself in the person of the Son. The type falls short because Eliphaz makes Job's gold a wager, giving up a fortune in the hope of getting it back.

study.christ:
This speech leads to Christ first as a mirror. Eliphaz says of a righteous man what the world said of Jesus: he is wicked, his iniquities are endless, verse 5. The high priests sought false testimony, Matthew 26:59, and the crowds charged Him with crimes He never committed. Job's position, blameless and accused, is one the Gospels show in full. Isaiah 53:9 says of the Servant that He had done no violence, nor was any deceit in His mouth, and yet He was assigned a grave with the wicked. The Christ who suffers is not the guilty man Eliphaz imagines, but the innocent one standing where Job stands.

It leads to Christ through the very list of sins. Eliphaz says Job gave no water to the weary, no bread to the hungry, no clothing to the naked. Jesus makes these the marks of the sheep at the last judgment, and identifies Himself with the people in need: 'whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers of Mine, you did for Me,' Matthew 25:35-40. The Christ who stands with the hungry and the naked is the answer to the man Eliphaz describes. And He is the one who fed the hungry, gave drink to the thirsty, and clothed the ashamed, so the gospel meets each item on the list.

It leads to Christ by the offer at its end. Eliphaz says, 'Reconcile now and be at peace with Him,' and promises that good will follow. The New Testament shows that peace is not the reward of a repentance well performed but the fruit of Christ's work. He is 'our peace,' Ephesians 2:14, and reconciles by the blood of His cross, Colossians 1:20. Eliphaz places the burden on Job; the gospel places it on Christ. This is the sharpest contrast, and it clarifies why Eliphaz's beautiful words cannot heal Job: they are advice for the guilty given to the innocent, and even for the guilty, advice is not enough.

There is also an unintended prophecy. Eliphaz says God will deliver the not-innocent 'through the cleanness of your hands,' verse 30. Job's clean hands do, at the end, intercede for the men who wronged him, 42:8-9. The pattern is completed in the one who prays 'Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing,' Luke 23:34, and who 'always lives to intercede,' Hebrews 7:25. Job, wronged and praying for his wrongers, is a signpost that points ahead.

A caution keeps the reading honest. Eliphaz is not a prophet, and Job is not Christ; the book never presents him as sinless in the absolute sense. The links here rest on shared patterns the New Testament draws for itself: the false accusation of the innocent, the wrongful use of God's name, and the priestly intercession of one who is wronged. In every case Christ does more than Job could, and does it perfectly.
study.god:
The chapter begins with a true statement about God that the rest of the Bible confirms. He does not need us. 'If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world is Mine,' God says in Psalm 50:12. Paul tells the Athenians that God is not served by human hands 'as if He needed anything, because He Himself gives everyone life and breath,' Acts 17:25. Nothing anyone gives God is something He lacked. That is the ground of grace: God's love is free precisely because it is not a purchase.

Eliphaz draws the wrong conclusion. He thinks that if God needs nothing from us, He has no reason to care what we do, and so any suffering must be a penalty for wickedness. But the God of the Bible is both self-sufficient and passionately interested. He is the God who hears the cry of the widow and the orphan, Exodus 22:22-24, who is a refuge for the oppressed, Psalm 9:9, and who repays kindness done to the poor as a loan made to Him, Proverbs 19:17. His independence is what makes His concern for the weak a matter of pure grace.

The chapter also shows a God who is not distant or blind. Eliphaz quotes Job as saying that thick clouds keep God from seeing, verses 13 and 14. Job never said this, and the Psalms and Jeremiah show what God thinks of the idea. 'He who formed the eye, can He not see?' Psalm 94:9, and 'Can a man hide in secret places where I cannot see him?' Jeremiah 23:24. The height of God, which Eliphaz uses to prove His remoteness, is the very thing that lets Him see all.

Most of all, the chapter shows a God who defends the truth about Himself. God says at the end of the book that Eliphaz and his friends 'have not spoken about Me accurately,' 42:7. It matters to God not only that people obey Him, but that they speak truly of Him and of His servants. This is a sobering thought for anyone who speaks for God. A false word said in His name, however pious, is a wrong that He takes seriously enough to require a sacrifice.

And it shows a God who is willing to use the man they wronged to bring grace to them. He will accept Job's prayer for the friends and not deal with them according to their folly, 42:8. The God who is angry at their speech is also the God who makes a way for their pardon. For worship, the chapter teaches us to be truthful about God, humble in accusing others, and glad that the Judge of all the earth is also the one who receives the prayers of the wronged for those who have wronged them.

crossReferences.note: Job's oath of innocence answers Eliphaz's charges one by one: he has not denied the poor, allowed the widow's eyes to fail, or let a needy man go without a cloak. If he has lifted his hand against the fatherless, he asks that his arm fall from its socket. The reply confirms that Eliphaz's list was invented.

God turns His wrath on Eliphaz and his friends because they have not spoken accurately of Him, and tells them to bring a sacrifice while Job prays for them. The book's final verdict on this speech is that its accusation was false and that the accused man becomes the friends' intercessor.

A cloak taken as a pledge must be returned by sundown, because it is the poor man's only covering and God is compassionate. It is the law behind Eliphaz's charge in verse 6, and it shows that the sin he names was recognised and legislated against in Israel.

The fast the LORD chooses is to break wicked chains, share bread with the hungry, bring the homeless in and clothe the naked. It is the positive image of Eliphaz's list, and it shows that such deeds are the mark of true devotion, not a private matter.

The King welcomes those who fed the hungry, gave drink to the thirsty, clothed the naked and visited the prisoner, and says they did it to Him. Jesus turns Eliphaz's imagined crimes into the criterion of judgment, and identifies Himself with the needy.

The wicked say 'The LORD does not see,' and the psalmist answers that the one who formed the eye can surely see. This is the reply to Eliphaz's claim in verses 13 and 14 that Job thinks God is hidden by thick clouds.

Paul says God is not served by human hands as though He needed anything. It confirms Eliphaz's opening claim in verses 2 and 3 and shows how it belongs to grace, not to the conclusion that God is indifferent to human conduct.

The chief priests and the whole Sanhedrin seek false testimony against Jesus, and two witnesses come forward with a garbled charge. The pattern of an innocent man accused in God's name by those who claim to know His will is the Gospel counterpart of Eliphaz and Job.

Christ Himself is our peace and has torn down the wall of hostility. It gives Eliphaz's appeal in verse 21 to 'be at peace with Him' its true foundation. Peace with God comes as a gift secured by another, not as the reward for a sinner's repentance.

Christ always lives to intercede for those who draw near to God through Him. It carries to its height the promise Eliphaz half sees in verse 30, that the clean hands of one person can rescue another, and the pattern Job displays in praying for the friends.

study.oneStory:
Eliphaz's speech belongs to the long conversation in Scripture about how a holy God relates to a suffering world. It answers something from the beginning: after Genesis 3, human beings quickly assume that God's favour and disfavour can be read from outward circumstances. Cain's offering, Joseph's brothers, Israel in the wilderness, all tempt people to draw a line between hardship and guilt. Eliphaz is the most articulate voice of that instinct, and the book of Job exists partly to break it.

The chapter also sets up what comes next. Job's reply in chapters 23 and 24 abandons the friends and turns toward God, and chapter 31 will answer these false charges with a sworn defence. Then the whirlwind speeches will show that the friends' God was too small, and the epilogue will vindicate Job. So the sequence moves from accusation to appeal, from appeal to oath, from oath to God's own voice.

The rest of the Bible takes the two halves of Eliphaz's speech and sets each in its place. The list of sins is taken up by the prophets and by Jesus, who makes care for the hungry and the naked the mark of the people of the King, Matthew 25:35-40. The offer of reconciliation is taken up by the gospel, but with the burden lifted: Christ is our peace, Ephesians 2:14, and it is God who reconciles, not the sinner who earns it, Colossians 1:20. Job's clean hands find their fullest form in the priest who lives to intercede, Hebrews 7:25.

The false accusation of a righteous man reaches its climax at the trial of Jesus, Matthew 26:59-61, and the answer is His resurrection. It is the vindication that Job glimpsed in 19:25 and that the epilogue foreshadows. The story ends in the new creation, where the accuser is finally cast out, Revelation 12:10, and where no one will be falsely blamed for another's sins. God's servants will see His face, Revelation 22:4, and the God whom Eliphaz called distant and hidden will be known as He is, close and kind.

sermon.title: Job: Wrestling with Suffering
sermon.why: Piper's sermon on Job 2:11-31:40 walks through all three speech cycles and specifically quotes Eliphaz's final speech in chapter 22, showing how 'this is so preposterous' that Bildad and Zophar can barely continue after it, tracing the collapse of the friends' theology of retribution.

quiz.q: What is the basic problem with Eliphaz's accusations in 22:6-9?

options.text: They are invented charges with no support in the story, later denied by Job under oath.
options.note: Job answers each of these very charges in chapter 31, and God rebukes Eliphaz's speech in 42:7.

options.text: They are somewhat exaggerated but based on real faults in Job.
options.note: The text gives no basis for any of these charges; they are not exaggerations of real faults.

options.text: They are general warnings, not meant as specific accusations.
options.note: The language is specific and personal, aimed squarely at Job, not general.

options.text: They are proven true later in the book.
options.note: The opposite happens; God vindicates Job and rebukes Eliphaz.

quiz.q: Why does Eliphaz's opening question in 22:2-3 matter?

options.text: It rightly notes God's self sufficiency, then wrongly uses that truth to conclude Job's suffering must be deserved.
options.note: The premise is true, God needs nothing from us, but the conclusion drawn from it does not follow.

options.text: It proves God is indifferent to human righteousness altogether.
options.note: God's self sufficiency does not mean indifference; the book shows God deeply engaged with Job.

options.text: It is simply false and has no theological value.
options.note: The premise about God's self sufficiency is itself sound biblical teaching.

options.text: It shows Eliphaz has abandoned belief in God.
options.note: Eliphaz remains a fervent believer; his error is application, not unbelief.

quiz.q: What does God ultimately say about Eliphaz's speeches, according to 42:7?

options.text: Eliphaz and his two friends had not spoken of God what is right, as Job had.
options.note: This is God's direct verdict, requiring the friends to be reconciled through Job's intercession.

options.text: Eliphaz spoke perfectly and only Job needed correction.
options.note: The opposite is stated; Eliphaz is the one rebuked.

options.text: Both Job and Eliphaz were equally wrong.
options.note: God singles out the three friends for correction, not Job.

options.text: God rebukes the three friends by name, though Job too was corrected for presumption earlier in the whirlwind speeches.
options.note: True that Job was humbled earlier, but 42:7 itself is a direct, positive verdict that Job specifically spoke rightly about God.

quiz.q: How should the true counsel in 22:21-27, reconcile with God and treasure His words, be read?

options.text: As genuine wisdom in itself, misapplied to a man who had no sin of this kind to repent of.
options.note: Scripture can carry true statements in a flawed speech; the failure here is application, not content.

options.text: As proof that Job really was living in unrepented sin.
options.note: The narrative and God's own verdict contradict this reading.

options.text: As worthless because Eliphaz said it.
options.note: The content itself echoes true wisdom found elsewhere in Scripture, even though misapplied.

options.text: As evidence Eliphaz secretly did not believe in God.
options.note: Eliphaz is a sincere believer whose theology has simply failed him here.

quiz.q: What does this chapter reveal about the danger of a rigid doctrine of retribution?

options.text: When it cannot explain the evidence, it will eventually manufacture evidence rather than be revised.
options.note: Eliphaz's invented charges are the clearest example in the book of this danger.

options.text: It always leads people away from belief in God.
options.note: Eliphaz remains devout throughout; the danger is cruelty, not unbelief.

options.text: It has no real danger since it is usually accurate.
options.note: The book systematically shows this doctrine fails to explain Job's case.

options.text: It mainly makes people speak more harshly, though it need not lead all the way to fabricating charges.
options.note: Eliphaz's case shows the danger can indeed escalate all the way to invented accusations, not just a harsher tone.

questions: Eliphaz began gently and ended by inventing crimes to defend his theology. Where might you be tempted to twist facts, or assume the worst about someone, to keep a tidy explanation intact?
Verses 21-27 contain real wisdom, wrongly aimed at an innocent man. How can you learn to receive true counsel without assuming every hard word about you must be deserved?
God later says Eliphaz did not speak rightly about Him, even though Eliphaz was sincere and articulate. What does this teach you about the difference between sounding right and being right?
Job was falsely accused in God's name by someone who believed he was helping. Have you ever been on the receiving end of that, or been tempted to do it to someone else?
Job's vindication came only in chapter 42, long after this speech. Where are you waiting for vindication now, and how does trusting God's justice change how you wait?

translationNotes.note: 'Be of use' renders a term for profit or benefit; Eliphaz's question assumes a transactional view of righteousness that the whole book will complicate.
The quoted words, 'What does God know, does He judge through thick darkness', are Eliphaz's caricature of what he imagines wicked men say, not anything Job has actually said.

These closing verses are notoriously difficult in Hebrew; the BSB rendering follows the sense that God saves the humble and even delivers the guilty through the intercession of a righteous man, a theme that anticipates Job's own intercessory role for his friends in 42:8-9.
